sections.title: Understanding the Problem
points: The application recommends profiles using preferences and distance. A match occurs when both users make a positive swipe.
Discovery can tolerate some stale data. Swipe handling needs coordination so concurrent positive swipes do not lose a match.

sections.title: Functional Requirements
points: Users can create profiles, set preferences, and choose a maximum distance.
Users can request a stack of eligible profiles.
Users can swipe yes or no on each profile. Both users receive a notification when their positive swipes form a match.
Photo uploads, chat after matching, and premium features are outside the initial scope.

sections.title: Non-functional Requirements
points: The stack should load in less than 300 ms. The scenario assumes 20 million daily users and about 100 daily swipes each.
Concurrent swipes must not lose a mutual match. A retry must not create a second match or duplicate visible notification.
Geographic queries and swipe-history checks must scale without scanning every profile or historical swipe for each request.

sections.title: Core Entities
points: UserProfile stores profile metadata and preferences. The current request supplies location because the user can move.
Swipe records the initiating user, target user, decision, and time.
Match connects two users. A canonical pair key can identify one match regardless of which user swiped last.
CandidateStack is a temporary list of recommended profiles. The service refreshes it when necessary.

sections.title: API
points: POST /profile updates the authenticated user's preferences and maximum distance.
GET /feed accepts current coordinates and returns another bounded stack. This recommendation flow does not require conventional page numbers.
POST /swipe/:userId records a decision about the target profile. Authentication identifies the user making the swipe.
The swipe response can report an immediate match. APNS or FCM notifies the user who swiped earlier.

sections.title: 1) Profiles and candidate stacks
points: The Profile Service stores profile settings in the Profile DB. The initial stack query reads that database directly.
The query filters candidates by preferences and location. The deep dive adds geographic indexes and a stack cache.
The final candidate filter excludes profiles that do not meet current rules or have already received a swipe.
A later design precomputes small stacks for active users. It refreshes them as users consume them or change preferences.

diagrams.caption: Users can create a profile with preferences (e.g. age range, interests) and specify a maximum distance.
Users can view a stack of potential matches

flows.title: Build the initial candidate stack
steps: The client sends its current location to the Profile Service through the API Gateway.
The Profile Service reads the user's saved preferences and maximum distance.
It queries the Profile DB for profiles within the requested area and preference filters.
It returns a bounded stack. The user can request another stack when the current one is nearly empty.

sections.title: 2) Swipes and matches
points: The Swipe Service persists the decision in Cassandra. It checks whether the target user already made a positive reverse swipe.
A simple write and reverse-read sequence needs stronger coordination under concurrency. The deep dive adds atomic matching on a shared pair key.
A canonical pair ID and unique match constraint make repeated detection safe. The same pair should not create another match.
The second swiper sees the match in the response. APNS or FCM sends a push notification to the first swiper.

diagrams.caption: Users can swipe right / left on profiles one-by-one, to express "yes" or "no" on other users
Users get a match notification if they mutually swipe on each other

flows.title: Record a swipe and notify an existing reverse match
steps: Person A has previously swiped yes on Person B. Cassandra stores that decision.
Person B sends a yes decision about Person A to the Swipe Service.
The Swipe Service stores Person B's decision. It reads the existing reverse swipe.
If both decisions are yes, the service returns a match to Person B.
It sends a notification for Person A through APNS or FCM. The following deep dive handles simultaneous swipes safely.

sections.title: 1) Consistent low-latency swiping
points: A transactional store can protect a pair's swipe state and match decision when they share one transaction boundary.
A sorted pair of user IDs sends both directions to the same partition. Partition placement alone does not make separate operations atomic.
Cassandra lightweight transactions provide conditional operations within their supported scope. A normal batch cannot combine an arbitrary read and write transaction.
The illustrated Redis design atomically records one decision and reads the reverse decision with a Lua script. Cassandra retains durable history.
Redis failover can lose recent acknowledged writes. Durable capture, replay, and reconciliation are required before claiming failure-safe match guarantees.

flows.title: Check reciprocal decisions atomically in Redis
steps: The Swipe Service sorts the two user IDs to construct one canonical pair key.
It executes a Redis script for that key. The script writes the current decision and reads the other user's decision atomically.
If both decisions are positive, the application creates or retrieves the uniquely identified match.
It returns the match result to the current swiper. The notification path informs the other user.
Durable capture and replay must recover decisions and pending notifications after failure. A Redis acknowledgment alone does not prove this recovery guarantee.

sections.title: 2) Fast candidate generation
points: Elasticsearch can combine geographic and preference filters. Change data capture keeps its profile data aligned with the primary database.
Periodic jobs precompute stacks in the Stack Cache. Those stacks can become stale after location or preference changes.
The hybrid design serves cached candidates first. It queries Elasticsearch to replenish a low stack and applies current eligibility checks.
Stack size, expiration, and active-user thresholds limit background work. Significant preference or location changes trigger a refresh.

diagrams.caption: Use of Indexed Databases for Real-Time Querying
Combination of Pre-computation and Indexed Database

flows.title: Replenish a cached candidate stack
steps: The Profile Service checks the user's Stack Cache for eligible recommendations.
It serves a small batch from that cache. It triggers replenishment before the remaining stack becomes empty.
The replenishment job queries Elasticsearch with current location and preferences.
The service excludes previous swipes and updates the bounded stack. Profile changes reach Elasticsearch through change data capture.
A preference or location change invalidates stale candidates. Expiration and active-user policies limit unnecessary precomputation.

sections.title: 3) Exclude previous swipes
points: A full history query becomes expensive for users with many swipes.
The backend checks durable swipe history. A client-side Swipe Cache filters recent decisions that storage replicas may not yet expose.
A Bloom filter can reject likely previous swipes with little memory. False positives can hide profiles that the user has never seen.
Exact swipe records still determine matches. A Bloom filter cannot enumerate history and needs a rebuild after cache loss.

flows.title: Filter recent and historical decisions
steps: The backend queries the user's durable swipe history when it builds candidates.
It removes candidates whose IDs appear in that history.
The client receives the new stack. It checks candidates against its local recent Swipe Cache.
The client removes profiles swiped since the backend's snapshot. It records each new swipe in that local cache.

sections.title: Final Design
points: The Profile DB, Elasticsearch, and Stack Cache support profile discovery and replenishment.
The Swipe Service needs atomic matching and durable recovery. The Redis matching alternative appears in diagram 7.
Push notifications inform matched users. Client-side swipe history and optional Bloom filters reduce repeated recommendations.
